subjective.question: What is an advance organizer?
subjective.answer: An advance organizer is an introductory framework presented before the actual lesson that helps students link new material with what they already know. It is a brief overview, statement or set of concepts given at the start of the lesson which provides a structure for organizing the coming information, so that students can understand, retain and recall the new content more easily.

subjective.question: Define a positive classroom.
subjective.answer: A positive classroom is a learning environment in which students feel safe, respected, valued and motivated to learn. It is characterized by warm teacher-student relationships, clear rules and routines, encouragement and praise instead of fear and punishment, and active participation of all students in the teaching-learning process.

subjective.question: Explain strong control and laissez-faire approaches in the management of a large class.
subjective.answer: Strong control is an approach in which the teacher keeps firm authority over the class, sets clear rules and expects strict obedience; the classroom is treated like a sacred temple of learning where discipline is maintained through the teacher's control. Laissez-faire is the opposite approach, in which the teacher gives students maximum freedom, interferes very little and lets students make their own decisions. In a large class, strong control keeps order but may suppress participation, while a pure laissez-faire attitude can create noise and disorder; therefore a balanced use of both, according to the situation, is more effective in large classes.

subjective.question: What are the different kinds of outdoor activities? Briefly describe them.
subjective.answer: Outdoor activities are part of the curriculum but their realization is possible outside the classroom. Their main kinds are: (1) Field trips, in which students visit places of educational importance to observe real objects and processes; (2) Nature experiments, in which students explore and experiment with natural phenomena in an open environment; and (3) Research based studies of various phenomena, in which students collect information and data outside the classroom. These activities connect learning with real life and make it faster and more lasting.

subjective.question: How can a teacher promote social-emotional learning in the classroom?
subjective.answer: A teacher can promote social-emotional learning by building warm and secure relationships with students, by appreciating their feelings and teaching them to take control of their emotions, by encouraging cooperation, sharing and group work, by appreciating and praising good behaviour, and by integrating social and emotional development with academic skills in daily classroom activities. Counselling and early intervention by the school and the family also support students' social-emotional growth.

subjective.question: Explain some strategies to maintain discipline in the classroom.
subjective.answer: Important strategies to maintain discipline in the classroom include: setting clear rules and routines from the first day and communicating their positive and negative consequences; keeping students busy and actively engaged in worthwhile academic activities; using movement management to regulate the pace and flow of activities; giving praise and rewards for good behaviour; using group alerting and overlapping to keep students attentive; and intervening early, before a small problem becomes a serious misbehaviour.

subjective.question: Define formative assessment.
subjective.answer: Formative assessment is the assessment carried out during the teaching-learning process to monitor students' progress and understanding. It is regular and ongoing, for example through questioning, observation, class tasks and short quizzes. Its purpose is not to grade students but to identify their learning difficulties in time and to improve teaching through timely feedback.

subjective.question: Define self-control.
subjective.answer: Self-control is the ability of a student to regulate and manage his or her own behaviour, emotions and impulses according to the rules and expectations of the classroom without being constantly directed by the teacher. A student with self-control can wait for his turn, follow routines and avoid disruptive behaviour on his own.

subjective.question: What are the types of tasks given to students in the classroom?
subjective.answer: The tasks given to students in the classroom are generally of the following types: individual tasks, which a student completes alone; pair tasks, which two students complete together; group tasks, which a small group completes cooperatively; and whole-class tasks, in which the entire class works on the same activity under the teacher's direction. Tasks may also be written or oral, and short or extended, according to the lesson objectives.

subjective.question: What is constructive feedback?
subjective.answer: Constructive feedback is the information given to learners (or received by a teacher) about performance in a positive, specific and helpful manner. It tells what has been done well and what needs improvement, along with guidance on how to improve, instead of merely criticizing. Given proactively and in time, constructive feedback improves learning and classroom performance.

subjective.question: What is the role of a laissez-faire teacher in the classroom?
subjective.answer: A laissez-faire teacher gives students a great deal of freedom and interferes as little as possible in classroom activities. Such a teacher acts only as a facilitator or observer, does not impose strict rules or control, and allows students to make their own choices and decisions. The advantage is student independence and creativity, but the risk is loss of order and discipline if students misuse the freedom.

subjective.question: What are effective teaching skills? Define any two briefly.
subjective.answer: Effective teaching skills are the abilities that enable a teacher to manage the class and make learning successful, for example communication skills, questioning skills, movement management, group alerting, overlapping and giving feedback. (1) Communication skills: the ability to explain ideas clearly, listen to students and use verbal and non-verbal signals so that instructions and content are understood by all. (2) Movement management: the skill of regulating the pace and flow of classroom activities and transitions so that no time is wasted and students remain engaged.

subjective.question: The length of a task should depend upon what factors?
subjective.answer: The length of a task should depend upon the age and level of the students, the nature and difficulty of the task, the objectives of the lesson, and the attention span of the class. It should be long enough for students to complete the work meaningfully, but not so prolonged that students become bored, tired and distracted.

subjective.question: Write down the procedures for laboratory and project work.
subjective.answer: For laboratory and project work the teacher should: explain the objectives and instructions of the work clearly before it begins; divide students into groups and assign roles; make sure all materials and equipment are ready and available; state the safety rules and the rules of behaviour for the laboratory; supervise and monitor the groups while they work; manage time and movement so that work finishes within the period; and review and assess the completed work at the end.

subjective.question: Explain the importance of communication skills in classroom management.
subjective.answer: Communication skills are the basis of classroom management because every management action, such as explaining rules, giving instructions, questioning, feedback and dealing with misbehaviour, depends on communication. Clear verbal and non-verbal communication prevents misunderstanding and confusion, keeps students informed about expectations, builds a positive relationship between teacher and students, and helps the teacher control the class without conflict.

subjective.question: Being an authoritarian teacher, how can you manage the behaviour of students in the classroom?
subjective.answer: An authoritarian teacher manages behaviour through strong control: he sets strict rules, expects immediate obedience, uses his authority and power to regulate students, and applies negative consequences for non-compliance. He keeps a close watch on the class, does not allow questioning of his decisions, and maintains order through firmness and, when needed, psychological coercion. This produces an orderly and quiet classroom, although it may reduce students' freedom and participation.

subjective.question: How can negative reinforcement be used in the classroom? Give an example.
subjective.answer: Negative reinforcement is used by removing an unpleasant or disliked condition when a student shows the desired behaviour, which increases the chances of that behaviour being repeated. For example, if a teacher daily assigns extra drill work to the class but announces that students who complete their classwork neatly and on time will be exempted from the extra drill, students will try to complete their work properly to avoid the unpleasant task. The removal of the unpleasant task reinforces their good behaviour.

subjective.question: Why is the sequence of activities important in the classroom?
subjective.answer: The sequence of activities is important because a well-planned order keeps students busy, interested and on task throughout the lesson. Activities should provide variety in content, materials and behaviour, and less exciting or more demanding activities should be followed by preferred and more exciting ones, so that completing the first task is rewarded by the next activity. A proper sequence also manages transitions smoothly, saves time and prevents the free-time gaps in which misbehaviour usually occurs.

subjective.question: Describe overlapping in your own words.
subjective.answer: Overlapping is the teacher's ability to attend to two or more classroom activities or events at the same time. For example, a teacher who is helping one group with its work while simultaneously keeping an eye on the rest of the class and responding to a disturbance is using overlapping. It saves the teacher's time, keeps all students under supervision and prevents misbehaviour from spreading.

subjective.question: How can a reprimand be useful to control student behaviour?
subjective.answer: A reprimand is a brief verbal correction given to a student for misbehaviour. It is useful because it immediately informs the student that his behaviour is unacceptable, stops the misbehaviour before it spreads to others, and reminds the whole class of the rules. To be effective, a reprimand should be given in a normal tone of voice, without pointing a finger at the student, and it should target the behaviour, not the personality of the student.

subjective.question: Name three models of classroom management.
subjective.answer: Three well-known models of classroom management are: (1) the Preventive Management model, which focuses on preventing misbehaviour by teaching self-control strategies and planning rules, routines and engaging activities in advance; (2) the Logical Consequences model, in which students face the logical consequences of their misbehaviour, which is understood to arise from their unmet needs; and (3) the Assertive Discipline model, in which the teacher clearly states expectations and consistently applies rewards and consequences.

subjective.question: Explain why professional development is necessary for a teacher.
subjective.answer: Professional development is necessary for a teacher because knowledge never remains static; it keeps changing with time. It fine-tunes and improves the teacher's knowledge domains: content, pedagogical, management and social-emotional knowledge. Through professional development programmes a teacher refreshes and updates his techniques, learns current trends in education, assesses his own efficacy, and becomes a critical friend of himself and others. Since classroom management is a formidable part of every professional development programme, it also directly improves the teacher's ability to manage the classroom effectively.

subjective.question: Define predictive maintenance.
subjective.answer: Predictive maintenance is a type of maintenance in which the condition of school facilities and equipment is regularly monitored and assessed so that possible faults are predicted in advance and repaired before an actual breakdown occurs. It keeps the facilities in optimal working condition and prevents sudden failures.

subjective.question: How can an effective classroom be managed keeping in mind the population of the students?
subjective.answer: Keeping the population of the students in mind, an effective classroom can be managed by arranging seating so that all students can see well and there are no obstructions, by dividing a large class into groups for activities, by setting rules and routines that suit the number and age of students, by using group alerting and overlapping to keep every student attentive, by sequencing activities to avoid crowding and free-time disorder, and by giving individual attention and leadership roles to disruptive students so that the whole class remains engaged.
